content: In 2020, the prevalence of tuberculosis (TB) among women in Pakistan was 3%. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies Pakistan as a high TB burden country, with an incidence rate of 259 cases per 100,000 people in the same year. Smoking was estimated to contribute to 53,000 TB cases in men and 3,600 in women in 2020. Smoking not only increases the risk of developing TB but also worsens treatment outcomes and doubles the risk of TB-related mortality. Integrating TB treatment with tobacco cessation services is a priority under the WHO End TB Strategy. In Pakistan, a tailored smoking cessation program was developed for TB patients through a collaboration between the national TB program and the University of York. This intervention includes brief, 8-minute behavioral support sessions delivered by TB program staff, focusing on TB education, healthy behaviors, and strategies to quit smoking. Following a three-year trial called the TB & Tobacco trial, healthcare workers provided feedback to optimize the intervention before scaling it up. Changes included revising recording systems to document smoking status at registration and treatment completion, shortening training to half a day, and involving provincial TB program leaders. The trial demonstrated that 25% of TB patients successfully quit smoking, as confirmed by self-reports and biochemical verification at 6 and 12 months. Those who quit smoking showed better TB treatment outcomes, including higher sputum conversion rates, greater treatment success, and lower relapse rates compared to those who continued smoking. The intervention was subsequently scaled up to 59 out of 121 health facilities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, covering urban, rural, private, and public centers. Key factors for success included close collaboration between researchers and national/provincial programs, joint funding commitments, and consultations with healthcare workers to improve feasibility and acceptability. Advocacy and communication strategies were aligned across health programs to promote integrated, people-centered care for TB and its comorbidities. Primary healthcare (PHC) is central to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and should aim to decentralize and integrate services for TB and comorbidities at the primary care level. Integrated care models, such as one-stop-shop services, can reduce costs, improve efficiency, and enhance patient outcomes. Case studies highlight the benefits of integrated care. For example, in Georgia, a primary care-based screening program for TB, HIV, and hepatitis C (HCV) was introduced in 2018. This program increased screening coverage and linkage to care, with significant numbers of individuals diagnosed and treated for these conditions. Similarly, in Kenya, cough monitors were employed to improve the diagnosis of lung cancer among individuals with respiratory symptoms after ruling out TB. This initiative enhanced collaboration between TB and lung cancer programs, leading to earlier diagnoses and better outcomes. To scale up people-centered services for TB and comorbidities, collaborative planning and budgeting are essential. Advocacy efforts should engage a range of stakeholders, align communication strategies across programs, and address stigma and discrimination faced by affected populations.
